The flyers were everywhere. Tacked to lampposts, taped to shop windows, even stubbornly clinging to the windshield wipers of parked cars. "The Bramblewick Badgers – Join Our Team!" they proclaimed, featuring a cartoon badger in a surprisingly jaunty cycling helmet. Leo had been ignoring them, naturally. Leo ignored most things that required effort, particularly things that involved other people. His preferred activities involved comfortable chairs, good books, and the slow, deliberate consumption of Earl Grey tea. 

But the tournament was looming. The Bramblewick Annual Village Games, a spectacle of questionable athleticism and fierce local pride, was only a month away. And this year, his Aunt Mildred, a woman whose enthusiasm bordered on alarming, had decided Leo absolutely *had* to participate. "It'll do you good, Leo! Get you out of that dusty armchair! Fresh air! Camaraderie! A sense of community!" She'd declared, her voice rising with each exclamation point. He’d tried to explain that he wasn't particularly sporty, that his coordination was… rudimentary, that the mere thought of competitive anything brought on a mild anxiety. Mildred hadn't listened. 

So, here he was, standing awkwardly on the cracked asphalt of the Bramblewick Recreation Ground, surrounded by a collection of individuals who looked like they'd been assembled from a particularly eccentric community theatre production. There was a woman in a lime-green tracksuit attempting to juggle beanbags, a man with an impressive handlebar moustache earnestly practicing his badminton serve, and a teenager who seemed permanently glued to his phone but occasionally tossed a frisbee with surprising accuracy. It was, in a word, unsettling.

He spotted a man with a clipboard near a dilapidated shed. “You must be Leo,” the man said, his voice surprisingly chipper. He wore a Badger’s cycling jersey, slightly too small, stretched taut across his belly. “Welcome to the Bramblewick Badgers! I’m Barry, the team captain and general all-rounder. What’s your skill set?” Leo blinked. “Skill set?” he repeated. “I… I read a lot?”

Barry’s smile didn’t falter. "Excellent! We always need someone to… uh… strategize. Yes, strategize! We’re a very strategic team, you see. We plan. We analyze. We… contemplate. Right, sign here, here, and here. And please initial beside ‘agrees to participate regardless of physical aptitude’.” Leo signed, feeling a familiar sense of doom settling in his stomach. 

He looked around, taking in the haphazard collection of equipment scattered across the field: rusty bicycles, a net held together with duct tape, a single, deflated volleyball. It was all so… earnest. So full of a hopeful, slightly chaotic energy that he, a creature of quiet corners and predictable routines, found both baffling and faintly irritating. 

Barry clapped him on the shoulder, nearly knocking him off balance. “Right! Let’s get you acquainted with the team! First up, meet Agnes! She’s our resident cycling champion, though she tends to talk to her bike.” He gestured towards a woman meticulously polishing a vintage bicycle with a feather duster. Agnes, upon noticing them, gave a curt nod and continued her ministrations. Leo wondered if he'd made a terrible mistake.
